content: Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide composed of randomly distributed ß-(1-4)-linked D-glucosamine (deacetylated units) and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (acetylated units). It has various commercial and potential biomedical applications. Chitosan is commercially produced by the deacetylation of chitin, which is a structural component found in the exoskeletons of crustaceans such as crabs and shrimp. The degree of deacetylation (%DA) can be measured using NMR spectroscopy, and commercial chitosans typically have a %DA ranging from 60% to 100%. This makes chitosan positively charged and soluble in acidic to neutral solutions, with its charge density dependent on pH and the %DA value. Chitosan is bioadhesive and readily binds to negatively charged surfaces, such as mucosal membranes. It enhances the transport of polar drugs across epithelial surfaces and is both biocompatible and biodegradable. Purified forms of chitosan are available for biomedical applications. Chitosan and its derivatives, such as trimethylchitosan (where the amino group is trimethylated), have been utilized in non-viral gene delivery. Trimethylchitosan, also known as quaternized chitosan, has demonstrated the ability to transfect breast cancer cells. An increased degree of trimethylation correlates with higher cytotoxicity, and at approximately 50% trimethylation, the derivative is most efficient for gene delivery. Oligomeric derivatives of chitosan (3-6 kDa) are relatively non-toxic and exhibit favorable gene delivery properties. Chitosan is primarily used as a plant growth enhancer and as a substance that improves plants' resistance to fungal infections. It is approved for use on a wide range of plants, both indoors and outdoors, by commercial growers and consumers. The active ingredient is derived from the shells of crustaceans, such as lobsters, crabs, and shrimp, as well as certain other organisms. Due to its low toxicity and natural abundance, chitosan is not expected to harm humans, pets, wildlife, or the environment when used as directed. In water processing engineering, chitosan is employed as part of filtration systems. It facilitates the aggregation of fine sediment particles, which are then removed during sand filtration. Chitosan also removes phosphorus, heavy metals, and oils from water, making it a valuable additive in filtration processes. While sand filtration alone can remove up to 50% of turbidity, the combination of chitosan with sand filtration can achieve up to 99% turbidity removal. Chitosan is also effective in other filtration scenarios where suspended particles need to be removed from liquids. Additionally, chitosan, in combination with agents like bentonite, gelatin, silica gel, or isinglass, is used to clarify beverages such as wine, mead, and beer. When added late in the brewing process, chitosan improves flocculation and removes yeast cells, fruit particles, and other debris that cause haziness. Chitosan combined with colloidal silica is becoming a popular fining agent for white wines, as it does not require acidic tannins (primarily found in red wines) for flocculation. Chitosan's properties enable it to rapidly clot blood, and it has recently been approved in the United States for use in bandages and other hemostatic agents. Chitosan purified from shrimp shells is used in granular hemostatic products like Celox, manufactured by Medtrade Biopolymers Inc. in Crewe, England, and in chitosan dressings produced by HemCon Medical Technologies Inc. in Portland, Oregon, USA. HemCon products have been shown to reduce blood loss compared to gauze dressings and improve patient survival rates. These products have been supplied to the United States Army and have been used on battlefields in Iraq. Chitosan is hypoallergenic and possesses natural antibacterial properties, further supporting its use in field bandages. Chitosan is often marketed in tablet form at health stores as a fat attractor, with claims that it can bind to fat in the digestive system and expel it from the body, aiding in weight loss. However, there is no scientific evidence to support these claims.
